The core contribution of this work lies in its bio-inspired approach, drawing from neural mechanisms to facilitate knowledge retention and transfer when new views are introduced. The authors identify the 'view forgetting phenomenon,' where traditional multi-view learning methods struggle to maintain knowledge from previous views when new ones are encountered. To mitigate this, HVOP constructs a Knowledge Transfer Space (KTS) and employs orthogonal projection to reduce interference between old and new views. This is achieved through the use of recursive lateral connections and Hebbian learning, which are inspired by the adaptability of the human brain. The KTS is dynamically updated using Hebbian learning, specifically Oja's rule, which is intended to approximate the principal components of the input data. The model is validated primarily on node classification tasks, demonstrating superior performance in knowledge retention and transfer compared to several baseline methods. The experimental results, presented across multiple datasets, suggest that HVOP effectively mitigates the view forgetting problem, leading to improved overall performance. The authors argue that their approach provides a more robust and adaptable solution for multi-view learning, particularly in dynamic environments where new views are continuously added. The paper's significance lies in its innovative integration of neuroscience-inspired mechanisms into a machine learning framework, offering a fresh perspective on handling the challenges of multi-view learning. By mimicking the brain's ability to integrate and retain information, HVOP presents a promising approach for improving the performance and adaptability of multi-view learning models. The paper's focus on a specific problem, view forgetting, and its bio-inspired solution, makes it a valuable contribution to the field, although there are several areas that could be improved to further strengthen its impact and applicability.
